reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: A neurosurgical and infective emergency in which a collection of pus in the epidural space can rapidly compress the spinal cord or cauda equina
The classic triad of back pain, fever, and neurological deficit is often incomplete, so a high index of suspicion is essential
Progression from localised back pain to root pain, then weakness and sphincter dysfunction, then paralysis can occur over hours to days
Staphylococcus aureus is the most frequent organism, often reaching the spine by haematogenous spread or by direct extension
Risk factors include diabetes, injection drug use, immunosuppression, indwelling catheters, recent spinal procedures, and bacteraemia
Urgent whole-spine MRI with contrast is the investigation of choice and may reveal additional non-contiguous collections
Management usually combines prompt surgical drainage with prolonged targeted antimicrobial therapy, though selected cases are managed medically
Neurological outcome is largely determined by the deficit at the time of intervention, so delay is the main preventable cause of permanent paralysis
reference.pathophysiology: Bacteria reach the spinal epidural space by haematogenous seeding (from skin, urinary, respiratory, or endovascular sources), by contiguous spread from vertebral osteomyelitis or discitis, or by direct inoculation during procedures. The abscess damages the cord through two mechanisms: direct mechanical compression and, importantly, vascular compromise causing ischaemic or venous infarction of the cord, which can produce deficits out of proportion to the degree of compression. The thoracic and lumbar regions are most often involved, and the collection may track over several vertebral levels.
additionalDifferentials: Vertebral osteomyelitis or discitis without abscess
Transverse myelitis or other inflammatory myelopathy
Herniated disc with cord or root compression
additionalInvestigations: Urgent contrast-enhanced MRI of the whole spine
Blood cultures before starting antimicrobials whenever feasible
Inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR) and full blood count
Culture of aspirated or surgically obtained pus for organism identification and sensitivities
Echocardiography and a search for a primary source when endocarditis or bacteraemia is suspected
HbA1c and screening for immunosuppression or injection drug use
redFlags: Any new neurological deficit with back pain and fever mandates emergency imaging and specialist referral
Rapidly progressive weakness, sensory level, or new sphincter dysfunction indicating impending or actual cord compression
Sepsis or haemodynamic instability from the underlying infection
Known immunosuppression, injection drug use, or recent spinal instrumentation with new spinal pain
reference.prognosis: Outcome hinges on the speed of diagnosis and decompression; patients treated before significant weakness often recover well, whereas established paralysis or delayed intervention frequently leaves permanent deficits, and severe sepsis carries appreciable mortality.
pitfalls: Waiting for the complete triad of pain, fever, and deficit before imaging, thereby losing critical time
Imaging only the symptomatic level and missing skip lesions elsewhere in the spine
Starting antibiotics before blood cultures in a stable patient and losing microbiological data
Attributing back pain to a benign musculoskeletal cause in a high-risk patient
Underestimating how quickly a stable neurological picture can deteriorate to irreversible paralysis
